content: Yellow fever is a severe illness caused by the yellow fever virus. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected mosquito and cannot be spread directly from person to person. The disease is prevalent in certain regions of Africa and South America. Yellow fever can lead to symptoms such as fever, flu-like illness, jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes), organ system failure (including liver, kidney, and respiratory failure), vomiting blood, and even death. Individuals with yellow fever often require hospitalization. The yellow fever vaccine is an effective way to prevent the disease. It is administered only at approved vaccination centers. After receiving the vaccine, you will be issued an International Certificate of Vaccination (commonly referred to as a yellow card), which must be validated by the vaccination center. This certificate becomes valid 10 days after vaccination and remains valid for 10 years. Certain countries require this certificate as proof of vaccination for entry. It is important to discuss your travel plans with your healthcare provider before getting vaccinated. Additionally, precautions such as using insect repellents containing up to 50% DEET and wearing protective clothing are recommended to reduce exposure to mosquitoes that may carry the virus. The yellow fever vaccine is recommended for individuals aged 9 months or older who are traveling to or living in areas where yellow fever is endemic or where vaccination is required. It is also recommended for those traveling to areas with a known risk of yellow fever transmission, even if vaccination is not mandatory. If you continue to live or travel in yellow fever-endemic areas, a booster dose of the vaccine is advised after 10 years. The vaccine can generally be administered alongside most other vaccines. Certain individuals should not receive the yellow fever vaccine. These include people who have had a life-threatening allergic reaction to eggs, chicken, gelatin, or a previous dose of the yellow fever vaccine; infants younger than 9 months of age (with exceptions for infants aged 6 to 8 months who cannot avoid travel to yellow fever areas, in which case vaccination should be discussed with a doctor); and pregnant or nursing women, who should avoid or postpone travel to yellow fever areas if possible. If travel cannot be avoided, vaccination should be discussed with a healthcare provider. Additionally, individuals with a history of immune system disorders (e.g., HIV/AIDS), those undergoing treatment with immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., steroids), cancer patients, individuals receiving cancer treatments (e.g., radiation or chemotherapy), and those with a history of thymus gland disorders (e.g., myasthenia gravis, DiGeorge syndrome, or thymoma) should consult their doctor before vaccination. People aged 65 or older should also discuss the risks and benefits of vaccination with their physician, considering their travel destination and potential exposure to the virus. If you cannot receive the vaccine for medical reasons and proof of vaccination is required for travel, your doctor can provide a waiver letter. However, you should also seek specific advice from the embassy of the country or countries you plan to visit. If vaccination is not an option, discuss alternative preventive measures with your doctor. Like any medical intervention, the yellow fever vaccine can cause side effects, though the risk of serious harm or death is extremely low. Mild side effects include soreness, redness, or swelling at the injection site, fever, and aches, which typically resolve within 5 to 10 days. These mild reactions occur in up to 25% of vaccine recipients. Severe reactions, though rare, include life-threatening allergic reactions (approximately 1 case per 131,000 doses), severe nervous system reactions (approximately 1 case per 150,000–250,000 doses), and life-threatening organ system failure (approximately 1 case per 200,000–300,000 doses, or 1 case per 40,000–50,000 doses in individuals aged 60 and older). More than half of those who experience these severe side effects may die. If you experience a moderate or severe reaction, such as high fever, behavioral changes, or flu-like symptoms within 1 to 30 days after vaccination, seek medical attention immediately. Signs of an allergic reaction include difficulty breathing, hoarseness or wheezing, hives, paleness, weakness, rapid heartbeat, or dizziness, which may occur within minutes to hours after the shot. If these symptoms occur, contact a doctor immediately and provide details about the reaction, including the date and time it occurred and when the vaccine was administered. You or your healthcare provider should report the reaction to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) by calling 1-800-822-7967 or visiting their website. In the rare event of a serious vaccine-related injury, the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) is available to help cover medical costs. For more information about the VICP, call 1-800-338-2382 or visit their website. For additional information about the yellow fever vaccine, consult your doctor or healthcare provider. They can provide the vaccine package insert or recommend other reliable sources. You can also contact your local or state health department’s immunization program or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) by calling 1-800-232-4636 (1-800-CDC-INFO) or visiting the National Immunization Program’s website.
